messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kayla was nineteen, an apprentice electrician just starting to feel confident behind the wheel, when a sedan ran a red light and slammed into the passenger side of her truck. She had been driving a coworker home, and in the split second before impact she remembered her hands frozen on the steering wheel, unable to swerve. The other driver sped away. Kayla survived with whiplash and bruises—her coworker was unharmed—but in the months afterward aquiet certainty settled into her bones: what happened was deeply unfair, and no one was ever held accountable. She also began to wonder whether she could have reacted differently, whether her body simply refused to do what she needed it to do at the moment that mattered most.

Returning to work as an electrician meant climbing into her truck again. At first the anxiety was manageable; she would grip the wheel a little tighter and remind herself that accidents were rare. But the triggers crept in sideways. One afternoon her supervisor asked her to drive a colleague to a job site across town, and as she pulled out of the lot with someone in the passenger seat she felt her stomach drop. The presence of another person in the vehicle, the weight of their safety, made every decision feel consequential. She began to think, *I can’t trust that I will do the right thing*—not just about driving, but about anything. That self-doubt followed her onto the work floor; when she was wiring a panel she second-guessed every connection. The trigger of driving with someone had fed directly into a deeper belief that she was no longer reliable.

And then that belief made her more sensitive to the world around her. After doubting her own judgment, Kayla started noticing every car that drifted too close to the center line, every dented bumper in the warehouse parking lot. The thought *I can’t trust my own body* surfaced whenever she braked for a yellow light and felt her leg tense too late. That appraisal—that her muscles and reflexes had betrayed her—sharpened her attention to potential collisions. She would see two cars stopped at an intersection and suddenly picture one of them lurching forward, the metal crunch she already knew. The crash imagery, the sight of cars that might be hit, became ever more frequent as she scanned for evidence that the world was as dangerous as she feared.

The injustice of the accident worked in a similar loop. When her foreman mentioned a long-term project that could lead to a promotion—talking about the future, something she used to do easily—Kayla felt a flash of anger. It was unfair that she had to carry this weight, that the driver who hit her got to go on with his life while she was stuck reliving a moment she never asked for. That sense of unfairness, in turn, made her hyperalert to any reminder of the crash. Later that same day she saw a news report about a multi-car pileup on the highway; the footage was brief, but it lodged in her mind and pulled her back into the feeling of her seatbelt catching. The trigger of crash imagery was more potent precisely because the appraisal of injustice had already primed her to see the world as a place where bad things happen without recompense.

By the time Kayla sought help she was twenty-one, still working the same job, but the loops had tightened. Every shift involved some combination of triggers—driving with people, glimpsing a damaged car, being asked to plan ahead—and each trigger reinforced the three beliefs that had calcified since the accident: that she could not trust herself, that what happened was deeply unfair, that her own body was an unreliable instrument. She had stopped talking about her own future altogether, not out of avoidance but because the thought led straight back to the unfairness, which then led back to noticing cars that might hit each other. It was exhausting. She came into the clinic hoping that somewhere in all this she could find a way to trust her own hands again, and maybe, eventually, drive without feeling that the next intersection held something waiting for her.
